Architecture design shifts from fixed workflows to scalable depth, width, connectivity, and growth protocols, yielding parameter-efficient modular computation for hierarchically decomposable tasks.
Experiments show NeuroMAS outperforms inference-time and trained baselines; scaling is path-dependent—progressive growth from smaller trained systems enables training of larger models.

bullets: Microservice systems rely on anomaly detection to maintain reliability, yet current multimodal methods ignore modality-specific traits and suffer from identity-shortcut issues.
LLMMAD embeds multimodal data into a unified sequence for LLM processing, uses modality-wise reconstruction heads, and predicts future states to eliminate identity-shortcut.
Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that LLMMAD outperforms existing approaches in multimodal anomaly detection for microservice systems.
Microservice systems need quick anomaly detection (finding unusual patterns); current methods ignore each data type and copy inputs, causing errors.
LLMMAD uses a Large Language Model (AI that reads language) to merge data types into one sequence, then predicts future states, keeping each type’s details.
Tests on three real datasets show LLMMAD outperforms existing methods, improving reliability of cloud applications.
LLMMAD uses LLM to embed multimodal microservice data into a unified sequence, modeling inter-modality relationships while preserving modality-specific info via reconstruction heads.
Implements prediction-driven autoregressive objective to avoid identity-shortcut, predicting future states instead of copying current inputs.
Evaluated on three real-world datasets, showing improved anomaly detection over existing multimodal methods.

bullets: Quasar links proposed API changes to actual consumer references, giving producers concrete evidence for release decisions.
It highlights the challenge of assessing downstream impact when a library change originates in one repo but affects many others.
The tool aids both producers and coding agents by revealing which consumers still rely on changed symbols, informing migration strategies.
Quasar links a library’s API change to actual usage in other projects, showing how many consumers still rely on the altered code.
This visibility helps producers decide whether to remove or keep a deprecated method, by revealing its “blast radius” – the spread of affected projects.
The tool also informs automated coding agents, giving them cross‑repository context to assess downstream risk and plan safe migrations.
Quasar links proposed API changes to observed consumer references across Netflix's shared Java libraries, giving producers concrete evidence of downstream impact.
The tool tracks API diffs, identifies remaining calls to deprecated methods, and maps consumer versions, enabling producers to assess risk before removal.
By exposing blast radius, Quasar supports automated agents in planning migrations and testing, reducing manual effort in large, independently evolving repository ecosystems.
